headline: Peconic porgies fire as bay water hits 72 degrees
subhead: Jumbo scup stack around Shelter Island while weakfish show in numbers for first time this season.
body_markdown:
The Peconic finally hit its stride this week as bay temperatures spiked to 72 degrees — a full 4 degrees warmer than the Sound side. That thermal gradient is doing exactly what it's supposed to do: stacking bait and firing up the porgy bite like I haven't seen since early May.

The jumbo scup are absolutely loaded around Shelter Island, particularly the deeper edges near the ferry run where the current keeps fresh water moving. I'm talking about legitimate 18-inch fish pushing 3 pounds, not the usual bay rats. The key has been anchoring in 25 to 30 feet on the flood tide with a steady chum slick of crushed clams. Simple high-low rigs with size 4 hooks and fresh clam strips are all you need, but the presentation matters — keep that bait moving just off bottom as the tide pushes through.

What's really got my attention is the weakfish showing up in numbers I haven't seen in years. The warming bay water has pulled them in from deeper water, and they're mixed right in with the porgies. I've been picking up 18 to 20-inch weaks consistently, with a few pushing 4 pounds. They're hitting the same clam baits as the porgies, but you'll know when you hook one — that head-shaking fight is unmistakable.

The striped bass bite has been more scattered but consistent for those willing to work for them. Early morning bucktailing around the deeper channels near Greenport has been producing slot fish in the 28 to 32-inch range. White and chartreuse 3/4-ounce bucktails with 5-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets are the ticket, worked slow on the drift during the last hour of the outgoing tide. The bass are relating to the thermocline that's set up around 20 feet — that's where the cooler Sound water meets the warmer bay water, and it's holding bait tight.

Three Mile Harbor has been a sleeper spot for fluke this week. The warming shallow water has pulled summer flounder into the back reaches where they're ambushing spearing and juvenile porgies. Bucktail and Gulp combinations in white and pink are working best, drifted along the channel edges in 12 to 18 feet. The fish aren't huge — mostly 16 to 19-inchers — but they're plentiful and aggressive.

The new moon we just passed really stirred things up with those big spring tides. The extra water movement flushed a lot of bait out of the back bays and concentrated it along the main channel edges. That's where I've been finding the most consistent action across all species.

Looking ahead, this weekend's weather should keep conditions stable with light winds and calm seas. The bay water should continue warming, which means the porgy bite will only get better. I'm expecting the weakfish numbers to increase as more fish move in from the Sound, and the early morning bass bite should remain solid as long as we keep getting that temperature differential between bay and Sound water.

The full moon coming up next week will bring another round of strong tides, which should really fire up the inlet fishing at Orient Point. That's when I'll be watching for the first real push of summer bluefish to show up in numbers.
